analysis.one_liner: Makes police chokeholds a federal civil rights violation.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a markup, a vote, or any action after its subcommittee referral in November 2018.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend a federal criminal civil rights law to say that any pressure on the throat or windpipe that can hinder breathing counts as punishment under color of law. That would let federal prosecutors charge police officers who use chokeholds with depriving someone of their civil rights. The bill never moved past the House Judiciary Committee before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People in police custody, especially those at risk of being choked or asphyxiated by officers. A federal civil rights charge would give prosecutors a tool when someone is injured or killed by a chokehold, on top of any state charges.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a sentence to 18 U.S.C. 242 stating that application of any pressure to the throat or windpipe which may prevent or hinder breathing or reduce intake of air is 'a punishment, pain, or penalty,' making a chokehold itself a deprivation of rights under color of law [S2][S3].

Because 18 U.S.C. 242 is the federal criminal civil rights statute covering willful deprivations of rights by people acting under government authority, this would apply to law enforcement officers and other government actors covered by that provision [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to forbid the use of chokeholds by persons subject to section 242's prohibitions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and agencies, which would face federal criminal exposure for using chokeholds, and potentially unions that defend officers in such cases.

drawbacks.text: The provision is a one-sentence definitional addition, so it does not by itself ban chokeholds in state law or limit state prosecutions; an officer could still face only a state charge unless federal prosecutors bring a 242 case [S3].
Federal civil rights charges under section 242 require proving willfulness, so the practical deterrent would depend on how aggressively federal prosecutors use it, which the bill does not change.

Police groups have generally opposed federal criminal standards for use of force, arguing officer conduct is already governed by state law and department policy; no such groups are named in the record for this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a clear federal criminal rule against a restraint technique that has killed people in police custody. The cost falls on officers who could face federal charges for chokeholds, which supporters would call the point of the bill. The main design limit is that the bill relies on existing federal prosecutorial discretion and does not change state law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, and no committee vote, floor vote, or any further action ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries introduced the bill on November 6, 2018 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On November 15, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and police unions are better off: no federal chokehold standard was created, and the existing rules governing use of force remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police officers and unions; the status quo held

for.name: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill making chokeholds a federal civil rights violation.

for.name: 17 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Nadler, Bass, Clarke, Clay, Cohen, DeLauro, and Lee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Bob Goodlatte)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after referral; the record shows no committee action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 15, 2018 and took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill; no Republican supported it in the record.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill would have exposed officers to federal criminal civil rights charges for using chokeholds. Police unions typically fight new criminal standards for use of force, though none are named in this record. For people in custody, a federal chokehold charge is a protection that currently does not exist.
